name: Hannya Mask
powers: Embodies a woman turned demon by jealousy
description: A Noh theatre mask sculpted as the face of a woman twisted by jealousy into a horned, serpent-eyed demon, with metal fangs and a grimacing mouth. Carried by performers in plays such as Dojoji and Aoi no Ue, the hannya shows obsession consuming the living into demonic form, and the mask itself is held to retain dangerous power.

name: Oni no Kanabo
powers: Said to crush any demon or mortal it strikes
description: The iron-studded club that Japanese tales and art place in the grip of the oni, the red-and-blue ogre of legend. Treated as a stock attribute of the ogre rather than a documented artifact, it appears in tales from Shuten-doji onward, its weight said to crush whatever it strikes; no historical example survives.

name: Shimenawa
powers: Marks off divine ground and repels impurity
description: A sacred rope twisted from rice straw and hung before shrines, torii gates, and sacred trees to mark off divine ground. Its origin is tied to the rope strung across the cave mouth after Amaterasu emerged, preventing the sun goddess from retreating; the shimenawa now seals off the kami's dwelling places from impurity.

name: Hagoromo
powers: Lets its wearer fly between heaven and earth
description: The feather mantle that lets a heavenly maiden (tennyo) fly between the mortal world and the sky. In the classic Noh play Hagoromo, a fisherman of Mio Bay finds one hung on a pine and makes the angel dance before returning it; the robe marks the tenuous boundary between human and divine realms in Japanese drama and folklore.
source: Noh play Hagoromo; coastal legend tradition

name: Kitsune's Crescent Comb
powers: Reveals a fox in human form; granting it service or love
description: The crescent-shaped comb that Japanese tales say a shapeshifting kitsune drops when its fox tail is betrayed. A man who finds one may gain the fox's love or service, and the comb recurs as the tell-tale clue in tales of fox wives whose disguise slips at midnight, linking the small hair ornament to the oldest fox legends of Japan.

name: Daruma Doll
powers: Talisman of perseverance and wish fulfillment
description: A rounded paper-mache doll modeled on Bodhidharma, the first Zen patriarch, whose hollow weighted body always rocks back upright. Bought as a talisman of perseverance, its eyes are inked one at a time as a wish is granted, and the year's dolls are burned in temple ceremonies that close out the warding of ill fortune.

name: Ruyi Jingu Bang
powers: Shrinks and grows at the wearer's will; weighs thirteen thousand five hundred catties
description: The magic staff of Sun Wukong the Monkey King, pulled from the East Sea Dragon Palace where it stood as a pillar weighing thirteen thousand five hundred catties. It shrank and grew at its bearer's will, and its gold-banded ends helped the Monkey King defy the heavenly host before he was pressed into escorting the pilgrim Tripitaka to the West.

name: Jiu Ding
powers: Signifies the Mandate of Heaven and legitimacy of rule
description: The nine bronze tripods (jiu ding) that culture hero Yu the Great is said to have cast from tribute metal gathered across the Nine Provinces, inscribing each region's creatures so the people could recognize them. Passed between the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties as the physical warrant of the Mandate of Heaven, they became the archetype of legitimate rule in Chinese historiography.

name: Hou Yi's Bow
powers: Shot down nine of the ten suns
description: The red bow of the legendary archer Hou Yi, who in Chinese myth shot down nine of the ten suns that scorched the earth, leaving one to light the day. His skill earned him the elixir of immortality, and his bow remains the emblem of marksmanship in tales of the heavenly archer and his doomed wife Chang'e.

name: Elixir of Immortality
powers: Bestows eternal life
description: The drug of immortality that Hou Yi obtained from the Queen Mother of the West. His wife Chang'e swallowed it to keep it from a thief and drifted to the moon, where she lives forever in the cold lunar palace with the jade rabbit; the tale, recorded in Han-era sources, gave the moon its goddess and the Mid-Autumn Festival its story.

name: Jade Rabbit's Mortar
powers: Pounds the elixir of immortality
description: The mortar and pestle with which the Jade Rabbit pounds the elixir of immortality on the moon, a familiar figure in Mid-Autumn Festival imagery. The rabbit is said to grind herbs under the cassia tree for Chang'e, and the same moon-rabbit motif recurs across East Asian lore, including Korean tales of a rabbit on the lunar surface.
source: Han bronze mirrors and moon-rabbit tradition

name: Bagua Mirror
powers: Deflects harmful energy (sha qi) and returns evil glances
description: A circular mirror ringed with the eight trigrams of the Book of Changes around a central yin-yang disc, hung over doorways in Chinese feng shui practice to turn away harmful energy (sha qi). Also paired with talismanic spells against hauntings, the bagua mirror is said to return an attacker's evil gaze and to guard the threshold from malign spirits.

name: Guan Dao
material: Steel blade on a long wooden shaft
powers: Emblem of martial protection and the god of war
description: The heavy curved-blade polearm historically carried by Guan Yu, the Three Kingdoms general deified as the god of war. The 'Green Dragon Crescent Blade' is the most famous of its kind; ceremonial guan dao are still kept in martial temples and used in lion-dance and martial-arts displays to invoke his protection.

name: Flaming Pearl
powers: Signifies wisdom, wealth, and transformation
description: A luminous pearl wreathed in flame (huozhu) depicted in Chinese art as the treasure two dragons chase or guard. Linked to the dragon's undersea realm and to Buddhist wish-granting jewels, the flaming pearl symbolizes wisdom, wealth, and transformation, and it appears on temple roofs, ceramics, and paintings across East Asia.
source: Dragon art motif; Buddhist jewel tradition

name: The Heavenly Loom
powers: Wove the patterned clouds of the sky
description: The celestial loom of Zhinü, the Weaver Girl, who wove the patterned clouds of the sky beside the Heavenly River. When her marriage to the cowherd Niulang made her neglect her weaving, the Jade Emperor separated the pair, and on the seventh night of the seventh month magpies bridge the river for their yearly reunion, the origin of the Qixi festival.
source: Qixi legend; Han to Tang sources

name: Cheonbuin
powers: Marks the royal mandate of the founder king
description: The heavenly seal that the Samguk Yusa says Hwanung, son of the sky god Hwanin, carried when he descended to Mount Taebaek with three seals to govern the world. Given to his descendants as the mark of royal mandate, the seal anchors the Dangun foundation myth in which the bear-woman Ungnyeo's son Dangun founded the first Korean kingdom.

name: Geobukseon
powers: Iron-roofed warship that shed fire and boarding parties
description: The armored turtle warship built for Admiral Yi Sun-sin's fleet in the 1590s, roofed with an iron-studded shell that shed flame and repelled boarders. Though a real historical vessel, it passed into Korean folklore as an invincible protector of the coast, celebrated in songs and tales of the Imjin War against the Japanese invasion.

name: Gogok
powers: Symbol of rank, fertility, and the sun
description: The comma-shaped jade ornament threaded onto the gold crowns and belts of the Silla kingdom and excavated in numbers from the tombs of Gyeongju. Scholars link the curved bead to the bear-woman Ungnyeo's offering in the Dangun myth and to shamanic fertility symbolism; it remains the emblem of ancient Korean royal regalia.

name: Bangmangi
powers: Grants whatever the wielder wishes when struck
description: The magic club (bangmangi) of the Korean goblin dokkaebi, which in folktales grants whatever a person wishes when it strikes. Villagers trick the gullible dokkaebi into beating the club and losing it, or use it to draw endless food, gold, and healing; the club and its owner remain beloved fixtures of Korean storytelling.

name: Thuan Thien Sword
powers: Granted victory over the Ming invaders
description: The magic sword Thuan Thien ('Heaven's Will') given to the farmer-emperor Le Loi by the golden turtle god Kim Qui during his revolt against Ming rule. After his victory the turtle surfaced on Hoan Kiem Lake to reclaim the blade, giving the lake its name, the Lake of the Returned Sword.

name: Betel and Areca Tray
powers: Foundation of hospitality and marriage ritual
description: The tray that carries betel leaves, areca nut, and lime, the foundation of Vietnamese hospitality and marriage custom. In the founding legend, twin brothers Cao and Lang died for love of the same woman and became the areca tree and betel vine; chewing the combination remains a rite of respect, greeting, and kinship.
source: Betel and areca legend; folk custom

name: The Jade Emperor's Gong
powers: Summoned rain when struck by the frog
description: In a Vietnamese folk tale, a frog led a deputation of animals to heaven to complain that rain never fell, then beat the Jade Emperor's own bronze gong until the god sent rain. The gong is a story element rather than a documented artifact, and the tale survives chiefly through oral retellings across the Red River delta.

name: Co Loa Crossbow
powers: Each shot could slay thousands
description: The magic crossbow of An Duong Vuong, its trigger made from the golden turtle-claw that Kim Qui gave the king at Co Loa. Each shot could kill thousands, but when the king's daughter My Chau revealed the secret to her husband Trong Thuy, the stolen trigger lost the citadel to the enemy.

name: The Emerald Buddha's Robes
aliases: Royal Vestments of the Emerald Buddha
powers: Palladium of the Thai kingdom
description: The three robes of gold worn by the Emerald Buddha in the Wat Phra Kaew temple in Bangkok and changed at the turn of each season in a ceremony performed by the king. The jeweled garments, their alternation fixed by royal ritual, mark the image as the palladium of the Thai state and the axis of the kingdom's legitimacy.

name: The Naga's Jewel
powers: Grants wealth and kingship to its holder
description: The luminous gem that the naga, the great serpent of the Mekong, is said to guard in the watery underworld, granting wealth and kingship to whoever obtains it. Retold in Thai and Lao river lore, the jewel is also linked to the fireballs that rise from the river during the full moon festival of the eleventh lunar month.

name: The Bayon Smile
powers: The king's watchful presence over the kingdom
description: The colossal stone face-towers of the Bayon temple at Angkor Thom, carved in the 12th century under Jayavarman VII with serene, downcast smiles. Khmer legend reads the many faces as the king's presence watching over the kingdom from every direction, and the towers remain the emblem of Angkor's guardian gaze.

name: The Four White Umbrellas
powers: Emblems of the right to rule granted from above
description: The white-tiered umbrellas that the Burmese chronicles place among the regalia of the first kings, emblems of the right to rule granted from above. Their role in the creation tale of kingship binds earthly sovereignty to the nats, and umbrella standards still crown Burmese pagodas and throne halls as marks of sacred authority.

name: The Relic of That Phanom
powers: Focus of veneration; guardian presence of the Mekong
description: The relic of the Buddha's breastbone enshrined at That Phanom on the Mekong, the most revered stupa of Laos and northeastern Thailand. Lao legend holds that a naga king, Phanya Sithan, invited the monks and guarded the shrine site, binding the sacred chedi to the river's serpentine protectors.

name: Khaen
powers: Voice of lam song and festival celebration
description: The free-reed mouth organ of Laos built from rows of bamboo tubes bound around a wooden wind-chest, its drone-and-melody sound the soul of lam folk song. Played at festivals, rituals, and courtship, the khaen is credited by Lao tradition with shaping the speech and poetry of the people.

name: The Golden Whip of Genghis Khan
powers: Said to rally and reward warriors of the khan
description: The golden whip that legend says Genghis Khan carried, brandished to rally and reward his warriors, and in some tellings the source of his military genius. No such whip survives or is named in the Secret History; the story is a modern heroic retelling of the conqueror's rise rather than a documented relic.

name: The Whistling Arrow
powers: Signal whistle that directed cavalry maneuvers
description: The signal arrow of the Mongol armies, tipped with a drilled bone head that shrieked in flight, used by Genghis Khan's cavalry to direct charges and ambushes across the steppe. Described by Persian and Chinese chroniclers, the whistling arrow survives as a motif of the swift, coordinated warfare that built the empire.
source: Persian and Chinese chronicles of the Mongol campaigns

name: Morin Khuur
powers: Voice of the horse and the steppe
description: The two-stringed horse-head fiddle of Mongolia, its scroll carved as a horse's head and its strings and bow made of horsehair. Legend tells of a herdsman whose beloved horse was killed, and who made the fiddle from its remains to keep the horse's song alive; it is now an emblem of Mongolian national identity.

name: Tsagaan Tug
powers: Ensign of khanly authority and national unity
description: The white standard (tsagaan tug) that Mongol tradition honors as the ensign of Genghis Khan's lineage, kept at the mausoleum complex in Ordos and paraded with the nine black banners at the Naadam festival. Its horsehair crown and spear shaft mark the enduring authority of the steppe khans.

name: Phurba
powers: Pins down demons during exorcism rituals
description: The three-sided ritual dagger of Tibetan Buddhism, its pommel carved with a wrathful deity's head and its blade meant to pin down demonic forces. Used by lamas in exorcism, the phurba transfixes evil at the axis between the worlds, and inscribed iron examples survive in temple collections.
source: Tibetan tantric ritual tradition; temple collections

name: Prayer Wheel
material: Metal and wood over a paper scroll
powers: Releases mantra prayers with each turn
description: The cylindrical wheel, rolled or spun in the hand, that Tibetan Buddhist practice turns to release the mantras printed inside, each revolution sending the prayer for compassion into the world. Rows of wheels line temple and stupa walls, and the device descends from Indian and Tibetan ritual turning of sacred verses.

name: Yeouiju
powers: Grants wishes; lets the imugi become a dragon
description: The wish-granting jewel (yeouiju) of Korean lore, the prize that a serpent imugi must grasp to climb into dragonhood. Said to grant any wish to its holder, it appears in tales of serpents waiting years for the jewel to fall from the sky, as in the story of the imugi that lost it at the waterfall.

name: Macuahuitl
material: Wooden club edged with obsidian blades
powers: Slices through flesh in a single stroke; a mark of warrior rank.
description: A flat wooden sword edged with rows of razor-sharp obsidian blades, the signature weapon of Aztec warriors at the Spanish conquest. Chroniclers including Bernal Díaz describe its edge as sharp enough to behead a horse in one cut; codices and tribute lists record it as both a tool of war and a mark of rank. Captured enemies often carried the most ornate examples.
source: Conquistador chronicles (e.g. Bernal Díaz del Castillo)

name: Atlatl
material: Carved wood with antler or bone spur
powers: Hurls a dart with far greater force than an unaided arm.
description: A carved wooden device that hurls darts with far greater force than an unaided arm, used across Mesoamerica from the Olmec era to the Aztec empire. Spanish accounts and Aztec codices show warriors and hunters gripping the notched end while the dart rests in its socket, and its power is credited with punching through metal armor at short range.
source: Florentine Codex and early Spanish accounts

name: Xiuhuitzolli
material: Wood frame covered in turquoise mosaic
powers: Sign of divine kingship; only the tlatoani may wear it.
description: The pointed diadem of turquoise mosaic worn by Aztec tlatoque (rulers) as the supreme sign of sovereignty, its name meaning 'pointed thing of turquoise.' Colonial accounts record that the right to wear it came from the gods and passed with the kingship, and Motecuhzoma is said to have been crowned with one at his accession. Codex Mendoza images show it above a headband of the same mosaic.

name: Ehecailacacozcatl
powers: Command of the wind that sweeps the road before the rain gods.
description: The shell breast ornament of the wind god Quetzalcoatl, a spiral conch called ehecailacacozcatl ('wind jewel') worn at the throat and tied to the whirlwind that scatters rain and seeds. Aztec images of Quetzalcoatl-Ehecatl show the spiral shell, sometimes a cut conch worn as a pectoral, among his emblems; colonial texts connect it to his journeys sweeping the road before Tlaloc's rain.
